did_you_know.text: Did you know? The verse describes Ahasuerus as a king who imposed taxes both on the mainland and on the islands of the sea, thereby portraying the extent of his rule as described in the scroll.
Did you know? The explicit mention of the islands of the sea alongside the mainland indicates that the tax was imposed across different parts of the kingdom, on land and on the islands.

Did you know? The scroll directs the reader to the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia, where the deeds and accomplishments of Ahasuerus, as well as the greatness of Mordecai, were recorded.
Did you know? The verse connects Mordecai’s greatness with the king’s actions, stating that it was the king who elevated him.
Did you know? This chapter provides no further details about the deeds of Ahasuerus or the greatness of Mordecai; instead, the scroll refers to the royal records.
Did you know? Mordecai is described as “second-in-command to King Ahasuerus”—a senior position in the kingdom—and is also explicitly called “Mordecai the Jew.”
Did you know? The scroll describes Mordecai as a leader who was great among the Jews and well regarded by most of his fellow Jews, meaning that he held status and was respected by many of them.
Did you know? Mordecai’s aims are summarized in two expressions: “seeking the good of his people” and “speaking peace to all his descendants”—caring for the welfare of his people and pursuing peace.
